Arduino · Uno R3 · Lab 12

Analog Temperature and Room Indicators

Build a room-temperature display while keeping the sensor estimate, its limits, and the indicator rule separate.

Lab MaterialPracticePractice Quiz

What you will learn

  • Connect a TMP36 and convert its voltage into an approximate Celsius estimate.
  • State the ADC reference assumption and reject implausible estimates before averaging.
  • Drive a classroom room-setting indicator with explicit boundaries and invalid-data behaviour.

On your bench

  • Arduino Uno R3 and USB data cable
  • Identifiable Analog Devices TMP36 in the three-lead TO-92 package
  • 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor for supply bypass
  • Green and amber indicator LEDs, each with a 330 ohm resistor
  • 10k ohm potentiometer for Quiz 6
  • Breadboard and jumper wires

Meet the components

Recognise the parts in the photos, then follow the labelled task diagrams for connections.

Before you build

  • Upload one standalone sketch at a time. Disconnect USB before moving components, verify sensor orientation, and use a common ground. Leave D0/D1 free for USB Serial and leave AREF unconnected. Serial Monitor uses 9600 baud.
  • Use a TMP36, not a similarly shaped transistor, TMP35, or LM35. For the specified TO-92 part, pin 1 is +VS, pin 2 VOUT, and pin 3 GND. The manufacturer shows a bottom view; identify the numbered leads from that drawing before applying power.
  • Power the sensor from Uno 5V and connect VOUT to A0. Place the 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor across the sensor supply and ground, close to its leads. Do not put a pull-up resistor on its analog output.
  • DEFAULT uses the Uno R3 supply as the ADC reference. These exercises assume 5.0 V; actual USB-powered supply voltage can differ. Use V = raw × 5.0 / 1024 as the specified nominal estimate. The divisor reflects 1024 ADC steps, unlike mapping endpoints onto an arbitrary percentage scale.
  • Work only in ordinary room conditions. Keep the sensor away from board heat and direct sunlight when comparing room readings; allow it time to settle. No flames, heaters, or liquids are needed. This is a teaching indicator, not a medical, precision, or safety instrument.

Copy one task’s sketch into Arduino IDE at a time. Replace the previous sketch before uploading the next example.

Sensor Voltage and Celsius Conversion

Task 1 · Guided build

Read a temperature at the desk

The TMP36 has a nominal 0.500 V offset at 0 C and a slope of 0.010 V per degree Celsius. Subtract the offset before dividing by the slope. The ADC reports voltage relative to its reference, so a wrong reference assumption changes the estimate even if the sensor output is steady. With the specified 5 V scale, one ADC step represents about 0.49 C. Showing one decimal place does not promise that precision. The plausibility helper accepts estimates from −40 through 125 C; this range check can reject some faults but cannot certify correct wiring or identify every disconnected input. Use one ADC sample for every quantity on a report line. Acquiring separately for raw code and temperature could make them disagree because the input changed between reads. The bypass capacitor supports the local supply connection; it does not correct an erroneous reference assumption. Keep conversion labels visible so an unexpected final number can be traced back to its input and units. The sensor and ADC are different stages, with different error sources. Inspect each stage before deciding that a stable final value is correct.

  1. Build the complete sensor circuit shown. Verify the exact part and pin numbering before connecting USB, then upload the example.
  2. Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. Each report contains the raw code and estimated voltage, followed by Celsius or CHECK if the estimate is implausible.
  3. Observe ordinary room readings and let the sensor settle after movement. Compare repeatability separately from agreement with another thermometer; a stable number can still have systematic error.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const float referenceV = 5.0f; // Nominal DEFAULT reference; an explicit assumption.
float temperatureC(int raw) {
  float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
  return (volts - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float celsius) {
  return celsius >= -40.0f && celsius <= 125.0f;
}
unsigned long sampledAt = 0;
void setup() {
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  sampledAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - sampledAt >= 500UL) {
    sampledAt = now;
    int raw = analogRead(A0);
    float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
    float celsius = temperatureC(raw);
    Serial.print("raw="); Serial.print(raw);
    Serial.print(" V="); Serial.print(volts, 3);
    if (plausible(celsius)) {
      Serial.print(" C="); Serial.println(celsius, 1);
    } else {
      Serial.println(" CHECK"); // Do not publish an implausible estimate as temperature.
    }
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Temperature is calculated from the same ADC sample shown in that line. An implausible estimate is not printed as a valid temperature.
  • Small changes between neighbouring ADC codes are possible; extra displayed digits would not remove sensor or reference error.

Experiment

  • Using the stated voltage formula, explain how a reference value that is too large would affect an otherwise valid temperature estimate.

Averaging Valid Samples

Task 2 · Guided build

A calmer reading for a desk log

A mean can reduce some short-term fluctuation without correcting a fixed sensor offset or a wrong voltage reference. This program averages eight consecutive plausible Celsius estimates. It waits for eight real samples rather than filling an unfinished group with zeros. Any implausible sample prints CHECK and discards the partial group. The next plausible reading starts a fresh group. Because the conversion is linear, averaging converted samples is appropriate here. Reports describe a group collected over time, so they may respond more slowly than a single reading when conditions change. The counter describes how many real values are already in the sum. Increment it only after validation and reset count and sum together. A partial group must not be padded with zero. This version accumulates floating-point Celsius values. If accumulating many raw codes instead, choose a wide type: 128 possible ten-bit values can sum to 130944, beyond Uno signed int. Sampling schedule, stored sum, and completed reports are distinct state; none should silently substitute for the others.

  1. Reuse the complete TMP36 circuit. Upload this separate sketch and observe how often complete mean reports appear.
  2. The first sample occurs after 200 ms; each full group needs eight samples. Keep loop running without delay and record the actual pace of several reports.
  3. Exercise the rejection logic on paper with valid, valid, invalid, then eight valid estimates. Do not produce extreme temperatures or disconnect powered leads to create a test case.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const float referenceV = 5.0f; // Nominal DEFAULT reference; an explicit assumption.
float temperatureC(int raw) {
  float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
  return (volts - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float celsius) {
  return celsius >= -40.0f && celsius <= 125.0f;
}
unsigned long sampledAt = 0;
float totalC = 0.0f;
byte count = 0;
void setup() {
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  sampledAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - sampledAt >= 200UL) {
    sampledAt = now;
    float celsius = temperatureC(analogRead(A0));
    if (!plausible(celsius)) {
      totalC = 0.0f; count = 0;
      Serial.println("CHECK");
    } else {
      totalC += celsius;
      ++count;
      if (count == 8) {
        Serial.print("mean_C=");
        Serial.println(totalC / 8.0f, 1);
        totalC = 0.0f; count = 0; // Begin a fresh, non-overlapping group.
      }
    }
  }
}

Observe and check

  • No mean appears before a full group. After invalid data, old partial samples cannot contribute to the next mean.
  • Averaging may make the displayed series steadier, but it does not establish a more accurate reference voltage.

Experiment

  • Describe the response-time cost of doubling the group size while keeping the sampling interval unchanged.

Synthetic Boundary Tests

Task 3 · Guided build

Check conversion without stressing the sensor

Known inputs let you examine boundaries without producing extreme temperatures or moving powered wires. This sketch supplies simulated ADC codes to the ordinary conversion helper; it does not read A0. Adjacent codes around the accepted range show how continuous temperature limits interact with discrete measurements. An exact temperature boundary need not coincide with an integer ADC code. Keep simulated and measured data clearly labelled in your notes. A rejected code does not identify its physical cause: several faults or assumptions could produce an implausible estimate. Once the logic check is complete, restore a real acquisition sketch before describing output as room temperature. The array is finite, so setup prints each selected case once and loop has no repeating test. Unit conversion is another separate calculation: after validating Celsius, Fahrenheit is C*9.0/5.0+32.0. Converting units or printing more digits does not improve the original measurement.

  1. Upload the Serial-only test without changing the sensor circuit.
  2. Compare each pair of adjacent boundary codes.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const float referenceV = 5.0f; // Nominal DEFAULT reference; an explicit assumption.
float temperatureC(int raw) {
  float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
  return (volts - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float celsius) {
  return celsius >= -40.0f && celsius <= 125.0f;
}
const int codes[] = {0, 20, 21, 153, 358, 359, 1023};
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  for (byte i = 0; i < 7; ++i) {
    float c = temperatureC(codes[i]);
    Serial.print(codes[i]); Serial.print(" -> "); Serial.print(c, 3);
    Serial.println(plausible(c) ? " ACCEPT" : " CHECK");
  }
}
void loop() {}

Observe and check

  • Discrete steps can straddle a continuous limit.

Experiment

  • Convert a valid 25 C estimate to Fahrenheit.

Reference Assumptions

Task 4 · Guided build

Compare two interpretations of one sample

An ADC code represents a ratio to the reference. This experiment reads one code and interprets it using two hypothetical references, 5.0 V and 4.8 V. The electrical configuration remains DEFAULT; no AREF connection or supply change is requested. The second result is a sensitivity calculation, not a second calibrated measurement. Neither column proves the actual supply voltage. A reference parameter makes this assumption visible rather than burying it inside the formula. With one fixed positive code, increasing the assumed reference increases the inferred voltage and temperature. Averaging copies of that code cannot choose the correct assumption or remove its systematic effect. Keep the original code in the report and let the sensor settle under ordinary room conditions. If a later supervised measurement establishes an actual reference voltage, record that evidence separately. Do not choose a reference merely because its resulting temperature appears more comfortable.

  1. Upload the comparison sketch on the unchanged TMP36 circuit.
  2. Watch both columns alongside their shared raw code.
Arduino sketch · guided example
float convertWithReference(int raw, float referenceV) {
  return (raw * referenceV / 1024.0f - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float c) { return c >= -40.0f && c <= 125.0f; }
unsigned long sampledAt = 0;
void setup() {
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  sampledAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - sampledAt < 1000UL) return;
  sampledAt = now;
  int raw = analogRead(A0);
  float c5 = convertWithReference(raw, 5.0f);
  float c48 = convertWithReference(raw, 4.8f);
  if (!plausible(c5) || !plausible(c48)) { Serial.println("CHECK"); return; }
  Serial.print("raw="); Serial.print(raw);
  Serial.print(" assumed_5V_C="); Serial.print(c5, 2);
  Serial.print(" assumed_4.8V_C="); Serial.println(c48, 2);
}

Observe and check

  • Two interpretations are not two independent sensor observations.

Experiment

  • Explain why repeated code 153 cannot reveal the actual reference.

Group Mean and Spread

Task 5 · Guided build

Describe short-term desk variation

A mean and a range answer different questions. Two groups can share a mean while one varies more. This sketch reports the mean of four consecutive valid estimates and the difference between that group’s maximum and minimum. The span describes these observations; it is not an accuracy specification or a confidence interval. Initialize both extrema from the first valid sample. Starting the minimum at zero would create a false span for an ordinary room group. Invalid data discards the partial group, so a later first valid sample initializes fresh extrema. Groups do not overlap. Sampling interval matters: a span across roughly one second describes a different window from a span across an hour. Quiet readings may still share a sensor or reference offset; a wider span may reflect real change, quantization, electrical noise, or movement. Keep interpretation separate from the arithmetic and compare the two reported quantities together.

  1. Upload the group-summary sketch using unchanged wiring.
  2. Compare mean and span over several settled groups.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const float referenceV = 5.0f; // Nominal DEFAULT reference; an explicit assumption.
float temperatureC(int raw) {
  float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
  return (volts - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float celsius) {
  return celsius >= -40.0f && celsius <= 125.0f;
}
unsigned long sampledAt = 0;
byte count = 0;
float total = 0, low = 0, high = 0;
void setup() {
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  sampledAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - sampledAt < 250UL) return;
  sampledAt = now;
  float c = temperatureC(analogRead(A0));
  if (!plausible(c)) { count = 0; total = 0; Serial.println("CHECK"); return; }
  if (count == 0) { low = c; high = c; }
  if (c < low) low = c;
  if (c > high) high = c;
  total += c;
  ++count;
  if (count == 4) {
    Serial.print("mean_C="); Serial.print(total / 4.0f, 1);
    Serial.print(" group_span_C="); Serial.println(high - low, 1);
    count = 0; total = 0;
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Each group’s first observation establishes its extrema.

Experiment

  • Construct two new groups with equal means and different spans.

Sampling Pace and Report Delay

Task 6 · Explore and measure

Compare complete-group schedules

A smoother display is not necessarily a faster display. Teaching task 2 needs eight observations spaced by at least 200 ms, so its earliest complete report is 1600 ms after the starting timestamp. This guided experiment changes the group to four observations spaced by at least 250 ms, giving an earliest report at 1000 ms. Make three coordinated changes: the timing threshold, completion count, and divisor. Changing only the divisor produces an incorrect mean rather than a quicker result. Keep the invalid-group reset policy unchanged. Late loop passes may delay observations; the program remembers the actual acquisition time instead of inventing missed samples. Measure report intervals on your own hardware and distinguish those observations from the requested schedule. Group size, interval, and loop workload all affect response. None corrects a fixed conversion bias. Comparing two explicit configurations is more informative than claiming that an unspecified averaging operation makes a sensor better.

  1. Copy teaching task 2 and make the three specified changes.
  2. Upload and compare its report pace with the original.

Observe and check

  • The mean’s divisor matches the number of actual observations.

Experiment

  • Predict the earliest report for six observations 300 ms apart.

Baseline and Change

Task 7 · Guided build

Compare with the first desk group

A baseline supports a relative comparison. The first complete four-sample group in this sketch becomes the reference; later complete groups report their mean minus that baseline. The haveBaseline flag distinguishes an unknown reference from a legitimate numeric value, avoiding an invented starting temperature of zero. An invalid sample discards the partial group while preserving an established baseline. Resetting the board begins a new baseline experiment. Those policies determine which observations can be compared, so make them visible in a report. Differences still rely on sensor and reference assumptions. Subtraction can cancel a constant additive offset in an ideal model, but it does not certify accuracy or compensate for a changing voltage reference. Keep the component in ordinary room conditions and note movement or changed surroundings. A reported difference near zero means that two calculated group means are similar, not that their individual observations were identical. Keep original baseline and later means available when explaining a surprising change.

  1. Upload and wait for baseline_C before interpreting changes.
  2. Observe ordinary room behavior without heating or wetting the device.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const float referenceV = 5.0f; // Nominal DEFAULT reference; an explicit assumption.
float temperatureC(int raw) {
  float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
  return (volts - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float celsius) {
  return celsius >= -40.0f && celsius <= 125.0f;
}
unsigned long sampledAt = 0;
byte count = 0;
float total = 0, baseline = 0;
bool haveBaseline = false;
void setup() {
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  sampledAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - sampledAt < 200UL) return;
  sampledAt = now;
  float c = temperatureC(analogRead(A0));
  if (!plausible(c)) { count = 0; total = 0; Serial.println("CHECK"); return; }
  total += c;
  ++count;
  if (count == 4) {
    float mean = total / 4.0f;
    if (!haveBaseline) {
      baseline = mean; haveBaseline = true;
      Serial.print("baseline_C="); Serial.println(baseline, 1);
    } else {
      Serial.print("change_C="); Serial.println(mean - baseline, 1);
    }
    count = 0; total = 0;
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Relative reports begin only after a complete reference group.

Experiment

  • Explain why this policy preserves the baseline after an invalid sample.

Hysteresis and Memory

Task 8 · Guided build

Avoid a flickering warm-desk label

A single threshold may switch repeatedly when observations hover nearby. Hysteresis uses two thresholds and remembered state. Here at least 28 C turns the amber LED on, at most 26 C turns it off, and values strictly between preserve its previous state. The same 27 C value can therefore accompany either output depending on earlier readings. That is intentional memory, not an inconsistent comparison. Validity comes first: an implausible value clears the indication and remembered state. The LED is a classroom label for a chosen rule, not a heater control or a promise about comfort or safety. This example uses single samples so hysteresis can be inspected separately from averaging. Test exact limits on paper or with synthetic values instead of forcing extreme physical temperatures. State initialization matters too: startup is off, so entering the middle region before any high reading leaves it off. Think through both directions across the thresholds.

  1. Add the D6 LED branch and upload.
  2. Trace the illustrated sequence before observing ordinary room readings.
Arduino sketch · guided example
const float referenceV = 5.0f; // Nominal DEFAULT reference; an explicit assumption.
float temperatureC(int raw) {
  float volts = raw * referenceV / 1024.0f;
  return (volts - 0.500f) / 0.010f;
}
bool plausible(float celsius) {
  return celsius >= -40.0f && celsius <= 125.0f;
}
bool warm = false;
unsigned long sampledAt = 0;
void setup() {
  analogReference(DEFAULT);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  pinMode(6, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(6, LOW);
  sampledAt = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - sampledAt < 300UL) return;
  sampledAt = now;
  float c = temperatureC(analogRead(A0));
  if (!plausible(c)) { warm = false; digitalWrite(6, LOW); Serial.println("CHECK"); return; }
  if (c >= 28.0f) warm = true;
  else if (c <= 26.0f) warm = false;
  digitalWrite(6, warm ? HIGH : LOW);
  Serial.print("C="); Serial.print(c, 1);
  Serial.print(" warm="); Serial.println(warm ? 1 : 0);
}

Observe and check

  • Middle-band output depends on history; invalid data clears that history.

Experiment

  • Give two histories reaching 27 C with different outputs.
